sentences.text: Taniwhasaurus is an extinct genus of marine lizards known as mosasaurs that lived during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous.
It was a medium-sized mosasaur with a maximum estimated length of around 6.7 meters, making it shorter than its relative Tylosaurus.
The largest known specimen of T. oweni has a skull length of 86.9 cm and an estimated total body length of 6.72 meters.
The short, wide, and muscular humerus with paddle-shaped bones suggests Taniwhasaurus was an efficient swimmer.
The genus Taniwhasaurus was first described by the Scottish naturalist James Hector in 1874, following the discovery of the type species T. oweni in the 1860s at Haumuri Bluff in eastern New Zealand.
New material from Haumuri Bluff was discovered in 1999 and formally described by Michael W. Caldwell and colleagues in 2005.
Two species are currently recognized within the genus: T. antarcticus described by Novas et al. in 2002 and T. mikasaensis described by Caldwell et al. in 2008.
CT scans of T. antarcticus suggest that Taniwhasaurus likely possessed an electro-sensitive organ capable of detecting prey movements underwater, similar to modern aquatic predators.
Researchers hypothesize that the large snout foramina in Taniwhasaurus are correlated with its toothless snout, though this requires further validation.
T. antarcticus likely had a high capacity for lateral neck movement, but the muscles involved lacked significant strength.
Taniwhasaurus was a close relative of the genera Tylosaurus and Hainosaurus.
In 1888, Lydekker reclassified Taniwhasaurus as a junior synonym of the genus Platecarpus.
In 1971, Welles and Gregg placed Taniwhasaurus in the subfamily Tylosaurinae based on cranial similarities to Tylosaurus.
Taniwhasaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous, specifically the Campanian stage, with potential records from the Santonian stage in South Africa, Japan, and Russia.

The Conway Formation where T. oweni was found dates to the Upper Cretaceous, specifically the lower and middle Campanian stages, while another formation containing a specimen is dated to the Santonian-Campanian stage.
The geological formation containing the Antarctic specimen dates from the late Campanian to late Maastrichtian stages of the Upper Cretaceous.
Researchers concluded that Tylosaurus haumuriensis is a junior synonym of T. oweni because the differences between the two taxa are mainly due to size rather than distinct morphology.
Subsequent studies have expressed skepticism regarding the claim that a juvenile skull found in the Maastrichtian belongs to T. antarcticus.

In 2016, Paulina Jimenez-Huidobro proposed reclassifying T. capensis into the genus Taniwhasaurus based on skull characteristics, but in 2019 she and Caldwell noted the fossils were too poorly preserved for a definitive genus-level identification.
